sacred_paradoxes.title: The Ship of Theseus
sacred_paradoxes.thought: If every plank of a sacred vessel is replaced over time, does the original soul remain?

sacred_paradoxes.title: Plato's Cave
sacred_paradoxes.thought: Mortals mistake the flickering shadows upon the stone for the ultimate truth of reality.

sacred_paradoxes.title: Socratic Ignorance
sacred_paradoxes.thought: I know that I know nothing. True wisdom lies in knowing the limits of your mind.

questions.category: What do you believe about the universe?
questions.question: Which idea feels closest to your view?

options.text: A personal God created the world and cares what people do.
Many gods or spirits influence different parts of life.
The universe itself is divine or contains the divine.
A creator started the universe but does not intervene.
Nature and physical laws are all that exist.

questions.question: Where do you think life's purpose comes from?

options.text: It comes from God or a spiritual purpose.
It is built into nature or the order of the universe.
People create their own meaning through their choices.
There is no built-in meaning, and that is simply a fact.

questions.category: How do you decide what is true?
questions.question: What should we trust most when we disagree?

options.text: Evidence we can observe, test, and check.
Reason, reflection, and spiritual experience.
What a community, culture, or tradition has learned.

questions.category: How do you decide what is right?
questions.question: Which sounds most like your moral view?

options.text: Some actions are right or wrong because God says so.
What matters most is reducing harm and helping people.
Different cultures can have different valid values.
Living in balance with nature and other beings matters most.
Shared religious teachings give society a strong foundation.
People should be free to make their own values and lives.
Ideas about truth and normal behaviour are shaped by power and culture.

questions.category: What is your relationship with spirituality?
questions.question: Which description fits you best?

options.text: I believe in one God and a relationship with that God.
I connect with several gods, spirits, or sacred traditions.
I feel that everything is connected and part of one sacred reality.
I do not believe in anything beyond the physical world.
I am unsure, but I do not think we can know for certain.

questions.question: What best describes your attitude toward big answers?

options.text: Some truths are universal and do not depend on opinion.
There may be many truths, depending on the person or culture.
We may never find a final answer, so we must choose how to live.

monotheism.title: Monotheism
monotheism.summary: You are closest to belief in one personal God who created the universe and gives life moral direction.
monotheism.personalDescription: You believe that one personal God created the universe and that life has a moral direction. Often you look to faith, prayer, religious teaching, or divine purpose when you think about right and wrong.
monotheism.populationNote: Includes practicing and cultural adherents of Christianity, Islam, and Judaism. These figures describe affiliation, not the exact strength of a person's belief.

polytheism.title: Polytheism / Henotheism
polytheism.summary: You are closest to a world where several gods, spirits, or sacred beings shape different parts of reality.
polytheism.personalDescription: You believe that reality can include several gods, spirits, or sacred powers, each connected with different parts of life. Often you see tradition, ritual, nature, and local community as important ways of staying connected to the sacred.
polytheism.examples: Historical Greek and Norse religions, Shinto, and folk traditions
polytheism.religion: Shinto, folk and Indigenous religions, or traditional African religions
polytheism.populationNote: Many people combine folk or local traditions with another religion, so this category overlaps with other estimates.

pantheism.title: Pantheism & Panentheism
pantheism.summary: You are closest to the idea that reality is divine, or that the divine is present throughout and beyond the universe.
pantheism.personalDescription: You believe that everything is connected to something sacred, or that the divine is present throughout the universe and perhaps beyond it. Often you find meaning in harmony, nature, compassion, and a sense of oneness rather than in strict separation between the spiritual and physical worlds.
pantheism.examples: Advaita Vedanta, Taoism, Spinozism, and some forms of Stoicism
pantheism.populationNote: This is an estimate based on monistic and non-theistic currents within Hinduism, Buddhism, Taoism, and spiritual-but-not-religious communities.

naturalism.title: Naturalism & Physicalism
naturalism.summary: You are closest to the view that reality is made of nature, matter, energy, and physical laws, with knowledge grounded in evidence.
naturalism.personalDescription: You believe that nature, matter, energy, and physical laws are enough to explain reality. Often you trust evidence, testing, and clear reasoning, and you may build meaning through human relationships and shared wellbeing rather than religious belief.
naturalism.examples: Scientific realism, atheism, and secular humanism
naturalism.populationNote: This estimate maps closely to the global unaffiliated population. Not everyone in that group is a committed philosophical naturalist.

deism.title: Deism
deism.summary: You are closest to belief in a creator who set the universe in motion but does not normally intervene in it.
deism.personalDescription: You believe that a creator or higher intelligence may have started the universe, but does not normally intervene through miracles or organized revelation. Often you value reason, natural order, and personal conscience more than religious institutions.
deism.examples: Some Enlightenment thinkers, including Voltaire and Thomas Jefferson
deism.religion: Deism (a spiritual belief rather than an organized religion)
deism.populationNote: Deism is rarely offered as its own option in population surveys, so this is an approximate estimate.

existentialism.title: Existentialism & Nihilism
existentialism.summary: You are closest to the view that the universe does not hand us a guaranteed purpose, so people must face uncertainty and decide how to live.
existentialism.personalDescription: You believe that the universe may not provide a ready-made purpose, so people have to face uncertainty and decide how to live. Often you care about personal freedom, honesty, responsibility, and creating meaning through your own choices.
existentialism.populationNote: This is a broad estimate of people who see meaning as personal, created, uncertain, or absent; it is not a standard survey category.

postmodernism.title: Postmodernism & Relativism
postmodernism.summary: You are closest to the view that ideas about truth are shaped by language, culture, history, and power rather than one universal story.
postmodernism.personalDescription: You believe that ideas about truth, identity, and normal behaviour are shaped by language, culture, history, and power. Often you question universal explanations and pay attention to whose voice is included, excluded, or treated as authoritative.
postmodernism.populationNote: This is an intellectual and cultural framework rather than a standard religious identity, so the estimate is approximate.

stoic_rationalist.philosophical_thesis: Reality is governed by a rational cosmic structure (Logos). Virtue consists in understanding natural necessity, mastering internal judgment, and accepting the flow of external causality.

matching_philosophers.name: Marcus Aurelius
matching_philosophers.core_idea: Mastery over internal representation and resignation to universal reason.
matching_philosophers.key_quote: You have power over your mind — not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength.
matching_philosophers.detailed_summary:
Marcus Aurelius served as Roman Emperor while maintaining a private reflective journal now known as the 'Meditations'. His thought aligns with your emphasis on duty, self-control, and rational composure in the face of chaos.

He argued that suffering stems not from objective events, but from our subjective judgment of those events. By aligning the mind with universal reason (Logos) and recognizing what lies within our control versus what does not, a person achieves unshakeable inner tranquility (Ataraxia).

matching_philosophers.name: Socrates
matching_philosophers.core_idea: The unexamined life is not worth living; virtue is rooted in true knowledge.
matching_philosophers.key_quote: I know that I know nothing.
matching_philosophers.detailed_summary:
Socrates revolutionized philosophy by shifting inquiry from cosmology to human ethics and self-knowledge. Through dialectic cross-examination (the Socratic Method), he demonstrated that most unexamined beliefs are built upon flawed assumptions.

Socrates maintained that moral failing stems from ignorance rather than malice. To seek virtue, one must constantly interrogate their own assumptions, question societal orthodoxy, and embrace intellectual humility.

matching_philosophers.name: René Descartes
matching_philosophers.core_idea: Methodological doubt as the foundation of certainty and rational inquiry.
matching_philosophers.key_quote: Cogito, ergo sum. (I think, therefore I am.)
matching_philosophers.detailed_summary:
Descartes sought an immovable foundation for scientific knowledge by stripping away all beliefs that could possibly be doubted. By systematically doubting his senses, memory, and physical world, he arrived at an undeniable truth: the very act of doubting proves the existence of a thinking mind.

His rationalist approach established a fundamental division between the mind (res cogitans) and the physical world (res extensa), laying the philosophical framework for modern Western philosophy and scientific inquiry.

recommended_media.title: Meditations
recommended_media.short_desc: Private personal journals of the Roman Emperor reflecting on duty, mortality, and tranquility.
recommended_media.detailed_summary:
Written while on military campaign along the Danube frontier, 'Meditations' was never intended for publication. It stands as one of the greatest works of spiritual and ethical self-discipline ever written.

Across twelve books, Aurelius reminds himself to act with justice, abstain from petty grievances, view the cosmos as a single interconnected living entity, and maintain dignity amidst the fleeting nature of mortal existence.

recommended_media.title: The Matrix
recommended_media.short_desc: A sci-fi masterpiece exploring Descartes' Evil Demon and Plato's Cave allegory.
recommended_media.detailed_summary:
'The Matrix' translates classical epistemological dilemmas into modern cinematic lore. Computer hacker Neo discovers that what billions of humans perceive as 1999 reality is actually a neural simulation designed by artificial intelligence.

The film directly dramatizes Descartes' 'Method of Doubt' and Plato's 'Allegory of the Cave', questioning whether sensory experience can ever provide reliable proof of true reality without rational awakening.

recommended_media.title: The Enchiridion
recommended_media.short_desc: A short ancient handbook detailing the distinction between what we control and what we do not.
recommended_media.detailed_summary:
'The Enchiridion' (or Handbook) is a short collection of practical Stoic maxims compiled by Arrian, a student of the freed slave and philosopher Epictetus.

It focuses intensely on the 'Dichotomy of Control': separating things that belong to us (our opinions, desires, and aversions) from things that do not (our body, property, reputation, and public offices), serving as a definitive guide to achieving emotional immunity.

existential_absurdist.philosophical_thesis: The universe is devoid of inherent teleology or objective moral law. Human dignity emerges through heroic revolt: acknowledging the absurd while creating authentic personal meaning.

matching_philosophers.name: Albert Camus
matching_philosophers.core_idea: Living authentically in defiance of the universe's fundamental absurdity.
matching_philosophers.key_quote: In the midst of winter, I found there was, within me, an invincible summer.
matching_philosophers.detailed_summary:
Albert Camus defined 'the Absurd' as the fundamental conflict between the human desire for innate meaning and the cold, silent universe that refuses to provide it.

Rather than turning to physical suicide or 'philosophical suicide' (submitting to religious dogmas), Camus advocated for living fully, passionately, and authentically in defiance of meaninglessness. He immortalized this stance through the figure of Sisyphus.

matching_philosophers.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
matching_philosophers.core_idea: Re-evaluation of all values, Amor Fati, and the Will to Power.
matching_philosophers.key_quote: He who has a why to live can bear almost any how.
matching_philosophers.detailed_summary:
Nietzsche diagnosed the spiritual crisis of modern civilization resulting from the decline of traditional religious frameworks. He challenged inherited moral systems, advocating instead for individuals to forge their own values.

Through concepts like 'Amor Fati' (love of fate) and the 'Übermensch', Nietzsche urged human beings to affirm life completely—including its suffering—and to live as self-determining creators.

matching_philosophers.name: Jean-Paul Sartre
matching_philosophers.core_idea: Existence precedes essence; humans are condemned to be free.
matching_philosophers.key_quote: Man is condemned to be free; because once thrown into the world, he is responsible for everything he does.
matching_philosophers.detailed_summary:
Sartre formulated the foundational principle of atheistic existentialism: 'existence precedes essence'. Unlike an artifact designed for a specific purpose, humans exist first, encounter themselves in the world, and only afterwards define who they are through their choices.

Sartre argued that denying this radical freedom constitutes 'bad faith' (mauvaise foi). We bear total, inescapable responsibility for constructing our own identity and values.

recommended_media.title: The Stranger
recommended_media.short_desc: A landmark novel exploring detachment, truth, and societal hypocrisy through Meursault.
recommended_media.detailed_summary:
'The Stranger' tells the story of Meursault, an indifferent French Algerian who refuses to conform to social expectations or simulate emotional pretense.

After shooting an Arab man on a sun-drenched beach, Meursault is placed on trial not merely for the killing, but because he failed to cry at his mother's funeral. The novel serves as a powerful exploration of the absurd and human honesty.

recommended_media.title: Blade Runner 2049
recommended_media.short_desc: A masterpiece on artificial consciousness, manufactured memories, and choosing self-worth.
recommended_media.detailed_summary:
In a dystopian future, Officer K—a bioengineered replicant—discovers evidence that leads him to believe he might be a miraculous, naturally born child rather than a manufactured product.

When he ultimately learns he is not the chosen child, Officer K must confront true existential choice: whether to remain an obedient tool or to sacrifice himself for a cause he believes in, proving that authenticity is claimed through action.

recommended_media.title: The Myth of Sisyphus
recommended_media.short_desc: A seminal philosophical essay proposing heroic acceptance of endless, repetitive struggle.
recommended_media.detailed_summary:
'The Myth of Sisyphus' introduces Camus' philosophy of the Absurd. He analyzes Sisyphus, who was condemned by the gods to roll a massive boulder up a mountain for eternity, only to watch it roll back down every time it reaches the peak.

Camus concludes that Sisyphus' conscious awareness of his plight transforms his punishment into victory: 'One must imagine Sisyphus happy.'
